summary: Defines the tools needed to run multi-party chat rooms with the Message Session Relay Protocol, which negotiates sessions through SIP and SDP.

eli5.summary: A chat room works through a middle host so many people can talk at once.

subtitle: How to run a group chat room over MSRP, with private messages and nicknames, using SIP and SDP to set it up.

tldr.problem: MSRP carries instant messages inside a session between two peers, but nothing defined how many people could share one chat room, address a single member privately, or go by a nickname.
tldr.mechanism: Each participant joins a SIP conference and opens an MSRP session with an MSRP switch, which relays every Message/CPIM-wrapped message to the others. The RFC adds a NICKNAME method, a Use-Nickname header, four status codes and a 'chatroom' SDP attribute.
tldr.outcome: It gives interoperable chat room behaviour for MSRP and eases interworking with systems such as IRC and XMPP. It is a Proposed Standard and nothing in the unit metadata says it has been replaced.

today: RFC 7701 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2015. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP, RFC 4975) sends a series of instant messages (IMs) within a session. Two peers set such a session up with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Session Description Protocol (SDP). RFC 7701 extends this to multi-party chat, also called a chat room.

The design builds on the SIP conferencing framework, RFC 4353. In that framework a specialised user agent called a focus hosts the conference. Something must also relay each IM from one participant to the rest. The RFC points out that systems such as IRC (RFC 2810) and XMPP (RFC 6120) already offer chat rooms, and that specifying equivalent functions for MSRP eases interworking between them.

The RFC covers private messages and nickname management in centralized chat rooms. It calls its mechanisms a future-compatible short-term solution for MSRP centralized chat rooms.
sections.eli5: Texting between two people is easy. A group chat needs rules, like who passes your message to everyone else. This RFC writes those rules down.

sections.title: Motivations and Requirements
sections.content:
Conference frameworks already existed, but the RFC says the exact details of session-based instant messaging conferences were not well defined. It sets out eight requirements so that conference-aware and conference-unaware clients can interoperate and so that gateways to existing chat systems can be built.

  • Participants can join, leave and exchange IMs (REQ-1).
  • A recipient can tell who sent a message and who it was addressed to, whether the whole room or one person (REQ-2, REQ-3).
  • A message can go to a single participant, a private IM (REQ-4).
  • A participant can have a nickname and change it during the session (REQ-5, REQ-6).
  • A participant can be known only by an anonymous identifier (REQ-7).
  • Participants can learn the chat room's capabilities (REQ-8).
sections.eli5: Before building a clubhouse, the authors list what it must allow: talking to everyone, whispering to one friend, using a nickname, and knowing the rules of the room.

sections.title: How a Chat Room Is Put Together
sections.content:
Every chat room has its own SIP URI, and people join by sending an INVITE to it. The focus UA handles those invitations and keeps a SIP dialog with each participant. Each participant also sets up an MSRP session with the MSRP switch, a special MSRP endpoint. The sessions can pass through MSRP relays (RFC 4976).

The switch is like a conference mixer in that it handles a session with each participant and bridges them. Unlike a mixer, it does not mix anything. It only forwards messages. The focus and the switch need an interface between them, but that interface is out of scope.

All messages use the Message/CPIM wrapper (RFC 3862), which carries the sender and recipient addresses. To message the room, a participant sends an MSRP SEND request whose wrapper To header is the chat room URI. The switch then copies it to everyone else. A private IM has the recipient's URI in To instead.

The room's behaviour is governed by policy attributes: whether nicknames are accepted, whether private messages are allowed, whether the room is deleted when its creator leaves, whether one user may log in from several endpoints, whether TLS is forced, the largest message sent over a congested session, a chunk reception timer, and the list of wrapped media types accepted.
sections.eli5: The chat room is like a mailroom clerk. Everyone gives letters to the clerk, and the clerk makes copies for all the other people. The clerk never changes what the letters say.

sections.title: Creating, Joining and Deleting a Room
sections.content:
Creating and deleting a chat room use the methods of the SIP conferencing framework unchanged. Whether a room is deleted when its creator leaves, or by some out-of-band mechanism, depends on room policy. When it is deleted, the switch ends the MSRP sessions with everyone.

To join, a participant sends a SIP INVITE to the room URI and is authenticated with ordinary SIP means, such as client certificates or SIP Digest. All IMs must be wrapped in Message/CPIM, so the accept-types attribute in both the SDP offer and answer must include Message/CPIM. If it does not, the focus SHOULD reject the MSRP stream or the whole offer, for instance with a 488 response. The real payload types go in accept-wrapped-types.

Conference-aware clients notice that the peer is a focus from the isfocus feature tag in the Contact header of the answer. A client that wants anonymity can supply an anonymous URI or ask the focus for privacy. In that case the focus MUST expose the anonymous URI through the conference event package.
sections.eli5: To join, you knock on the room's door, show who you are, and say what kinds of messages you can read, like text or pictures. The room only lets you in if you agree to its message format.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Messages
sections.content:
For a regular message, the sender builds an MSRP SEND request and sets the wrapper To to the room URI and From to its own identifier (a SIP, tel or IM URI, or an anonymous URI). The switch SHOULD check that From is a valid participant. A wrapper with several To headers MUST be rejected with a 403. Otherwise the switch copies the request to every participant except the sender. It MUST NOT change the content, though it MAY re-chunk it, and it SHOULD NOT forward content of a media type the recipient does not accept.

For a private message, the sender puts exactly one recipient URI in To. The switch rejects an unknown recipient with 404 and a recipient that does not support private messages with 428, and otherwise sends the message only to that person. Multiple private recipients are not supported. The RFC suggests sending one private message per recipient instead.

The switch may start forwarding as soon as it has the wrapper headers, without waiting for the whole message. It then MUST remember the Message-ID and the list of recipients so that later chunks go to the same people, and it MUST start a chunk reception timer so that an abandoned message cannot exhaust storage. The timer value is local policy, and a value around 540 seconds, similar to a normal TCP timeout, is suggested rather than a few seconds. A message without a Message/CPIM wrapper gets a 415, and an invalid From gets a 403.

The RFC recommends that switches detect and avoid congestion. For example, a switch may mark a session as congested when its TCP send buffer is close to 80% full and then drop regular messages or refuse large ones for that user.
sections.eli5: When you shout to the room, the clerk gives everyone else a copy. When you whisper to one person, only that person gets it. If the clerk's hands are full because someone is slow, the clerk may skip big messages for them.

sections.title: Nicknames
sections.content:
A nickname is a user-chosen name that is unique inside a chat room, so that a participant can be referred to unambiguously. It is bound to a URI, so one user on several devices can use the same nickname.

To claim one, the participant sends a new MSRP NICKNAME request with a Use-Nickname header. The string must be between 1 and 1023 octets and is UTF-8. The switch prepares and compares it using the rules of RFC 7700. Failures return 403 if nicknames are not allowed, 424 if the header is malformed, and 425 if the name is reserved or already used by someone else. On success the switch returns 200.

Changing a nickname uses the same request, and the old one is released only after the new one is accepted with a 200. If the request fails, the current nickname stays. Sending an empty quoted string removes the nickname. Other participants learn nicknames through the conference event package, using the nickname attribute from RFC 6501 and RFC 6502.

The RFC notes that look-alike names such as BOY and B0Y are different nicknames that can mislead users. Chat rooms MAY provide a way to mitigate this.
sections.eli5: A nickname is a name tag. Two people can't wear the same tag in the same room, and you can swap yours for a new one, but your old tag only goes back on the rack once the new one is approved.

sections.title: The SDP chatroom Attribute and IANA
sections.content:
A participant needs to know what the room supports. Without that, it might send what it thinks is a private message that is delivered to everyone. The reverse also matters: a client without these extensions must not receive private messages, because it could not tell them from regular ones and its reply would go to the whole room. So the RFC defines a media-level SDP attribute, chatroom, used with TCP/MSRP or TCP/TLS/MSRP media.

The attribute is a declaration of what is supported and allowed by policy, not an offer/answer negotiation, so an answer need not be a subset of the offer. It can carry the tokens nickname and private-messages. Extra tokens are allowed: IETF extensions use a standard token, and private extensions use a reversed vendor DNS name. No IANA registry is created for them. The attribute can change in later offer/answer exchanges, and omitting it means the chat room procedures are disabled.

IANA registered the NICKNAME method, the Use-Nickname header, the chatroom SDP attribute and four MSRP status codes.
sections.eli5: The chatroom attribute is a sign on the door that lists the house rules, such as nicknames allowed and whispering allowed. Visitors read the sign before they try anything.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of MSRP apply. In addition, a chat room is by nature a potential denial-of-service accelerator because it takes one message and sends it to many. Implementers, switches in particular, ought to include anti-DoS features, but the RFC does not specify them.

A client that does not understand the isfocus tag may not realise its messages can go to many people. To reduce this, the switch SHOULD send such a client a regular message saying it is in a chat room, followed by the roster. Participants who want protection on the path to the switch can force MSRP over TLS, and the room may require it.

If someone takes over a nickname, private messages could go to the wrong person, so the switch MUST keep nicknames unique within a room. A room policy decides how long a released nickname stays reserved, for example so that a user who lost connectivity can come back. Recipients should be careful with rendered content such as HTML, scripts and phishing attempts, and endpoints SHOULD ask the user before acting on it. A TLS client certificate that contains a real name is not anonymous to the switch.
sections.eli5: A room that copies one message to many people can be misused to flood them, so it needs protection. Tags must not be stolen, or secret notes could go to the wrong person, and you should be careful about what a stranger's message asks your computer to do.
